projects.title: The Long Service
projects.description: Slow television with a public sector job inside it. You are the conductor of the Nordkapp–Lindesnes through service — day three of four, Trondheim to Lindesnes, 938 km, thirteen hours and six minutes at one second per second — and the whole screen is a cutaway of the moving train you are walking up and down. You are also an EL1, and the working day (09:00 to 17:06, the APS standard day) happens on a laptop on the tray table at seat 12A, four carriages from the PA handset. That distance is the game: the announcement is due in four minutes and you are at the buffet; the doors need working and you are mid-draft; a tunnel takes the Teams call and whatever you were part-way through with it. The inbox only goes up, the assurance template comes back returned at a higher version number, and the Question Time Brief has to clear eight desks by 16:00 while two in five send it back. Paste in your own real assurance questions and they become the template. Everything is drawn live — the country through the windows lit by your own local time, the body rocking on its springs, the wheels turning on the rail — and it all keeps running with the tab shut. Nothing goes wrong. The incident log stays empty on purpose.

projects.title: Potato Farmer
projects.description: A potato farming simulator played in real time — which begins at the agricultural revolution, in 10,000 BC. The aim is to be a potato farmer farming potatoes; the condition is that you must first get through the intervening 12,026 years at one second per second. A live Neolithic clock, a progress bar that needs a 1,000,000× microscope to appear to move, ticking countdowns to the invention of pottery and the arrival of the potato in Europe, a lineage of foragers who each die after fifteen years, a day/night hillside lit by your actual local time, and a fully implemented potato field that unlocks in the year 14,052. The clock runs whether the tab is open or not, and progress travels between devices by way of a self-validating key that encodes the save itself — no server, no account, and invented keys are refused. Nobody has won.

projects.title: Quotle
projects.description: A Wordle for famous quotes — over 1000 of them, in a separate database. The whole quote sits on one line of letter boxes; each guess is graded and stacks below the last, so you read down the columns to see what you've nailed. Colours work per word — a yellow only tells you a letter is in that word, never across the whole quote — and each wrong guess unlocks another clue. A universal Quote of the Day, then unlock a random one. Five tries, then copy an emoji scorecard (one square per letter) to share.

projects.title: How to Protect Profits
projects.description: A playable tribute to Dr Paul Hubbard — economist, conductor, and the APS's first Assistant Secretary for AI Delivery & Enablement. Take the baton as the Masked Economist: catch the sector profits and public value, dodge the hype and red tape, and conduct your way across five stages drawn from his thesis, his livestream, and the APS AI Plan 2025.

projects.title: Grand Theft Tokens VI - Vibe City
projects.description: A loving, entirely-original parody of a certain open-world crime game — built from boxes, math and AI jokes and rendered live with WebGL. Drive around neon-soaked Vibe City, commit version-control crimes, dodge a five-star wanted system, and hunt 25 hidden golden Attention Orbs. Runs entirely in your browser, nothing uploaded.

projects.title: Fable 5 Max Impression - Sorting Transformer
projects.description: A 107,840-parameter decoder-only transformer written from scratch in pure NumPy — hand-derived gradients, gradient-checked, and trained to sort lists of opaque tokens with no built-in notion of order. Its weights are embedded in the page and the forward pass runs live in your browser; watch the attention head light up the argsort circuit it discovered.

pages.title: Source — sortformer.py
pages.description: The full pure-NumPy implementation: hand-derived forward/backward passes, gradient check against finite differences, Adam, training loop, and the analysis that exports the figures and embedded weights.

pages.title: Training curves
pages.description: Live training run: log-scale loss and held-out exact-match accuracy climbing to ~100% as the model learns to sort.

pages.title: Attention map
pages.description: Layer 1 head 1 — the argsort circuit the model discovered: heat shows where it attends while emitting each sorted token, circles mark the ground-truth argsort.

projects.title: Speed Reader
projects.description: A speed-reading tool that uses the RSVP method to flash text one word at a time at a fixed focal point, highlighting each word's optimal recognition point; adjustable WPM, chunk size, sentence-boundary pauses, and keyboard controls.

projects.title: Cube Maker
projects.description: Drop in an image, wrap it onto a spinning 3D cube, pick a spin style and loop length, then export an animated GIF — all rendered with WebGL in the browser, nothing uploaded.

projects.title: Opus 4.8 Impression - Neural Playground
projects.description: A small multilayer perceptron trained live in the browser by hand-written backpropagation — watch tangled classes get pulled apart in the network's learned 2-D representation until a single line separates them.

projects.title: Gerrymandering Dynamics
projects.description: Four interactive explainers on how district lines and electoral systems turn votes into seats — and why disproportionality is not the same as an unfair (asymmetric) map.

pages.title: The Symmetry Test
pages.description: Fixed 60/40 electorate, only the lines move; cracking and packing vs the symmetry mirror, efficiency gap, partisan bias.

pages.title: Districting Lab
pages.description: 100 voters, five parties, 10 seats; pick a map and move the electorate to watch Gallagher disproportionality and symmetry.

pages.title: The Seats–Votes Curve
pages.description: Two-party model: responsiveness (rho) and bias (beta) separate disproportionality from unfairness.

pages.title: Seats–Votes Lab · N parties
pages.description: Multiparty seats–votes with shared responsiveness and per-party bias multipliers; structural fan vs gerrymander.
